chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, and a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad, both together from Ibn Mahbub, from Ibn Ri'ab, from Zurara, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him)

regarding a man who orders a man with the killing of a man, so he killed him. So he said: 'The one who killed him shall be killed for it (qisas), and the one who ordered his killing shall be imprisoned in prison until he dies.'

key_terms.الْآمِرُ: The one who gave the order — the instigator or mastermind of the killing, distinguished from the direct perpetrator
key_terms.يُحْبَسُ فِي السِّجْنِ حَتَّى يَمُوتَ: Imprisoned until death — life imprisonment as the punishment for the instigator, a lesser penalty than execution
key_terms.يُقْتَلُ بِهِ: He is killed for it — the standard formula for qisas (retaliatory execution), indicating the killer is executed as equal retaliation for the victim's life

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on hiring or ordering someone to commit murder in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (AS) rules on a case of murder by proxy: the direct killer is subject to qisas (retaliatory execution), while the instigator who ordered the killing faces life imprisonment until death. This distinction reflects classical Islamic jurisprudence's nuanced treatment of criminal liability, where the instigator does not receive the death penalty since the direct perpetrator bears primary responsibility for the act. The ruling addresses a question that Zurara, one of the most senior jurist-companions, brought to the Imam, indicating this was a jurisprudential matter requiring authoritative clarification.
